To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) using a backtranslation model to generate buggy versions of programs is an efficient way to obtain large amounts of training data for debugging, (2) using a backtransation model on a large corpus of buggy programs and their corresponding stack traces improves debugging accuracy, and (3) using a skeleton consisting of the buggy program's parent class, signatures, imports, and method bodies improves debugging accuracy, especially for buggy programs without stack traces.

we can use large pretrained transformers to automatically generate synthetic bugs, and then use the debugging information from these synthetic bugs to improve the ability of the same models to fix real bugs.

(1) using synthetic bugs improves the performance of a bug localization model by 10%; (2) using synthetic bugs and stack traces improves a bug-fixing model's performance on QuixBugs by over 50%; (3) using synthetic bugs, stack traces, and skeletons further improves the bug-fixing model by 20%; (4) using stack traces and skeletons further improves our model's performance on our own benchmark of 10K executable tests by 10% and 15
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: can a large pretrained transformer be finetuned on debugging information to produce a debugging model?

two main goals: first, to show that large transformers can be finetuned to debug programs, and second, to show that debugging is a task that can be made significantly easier by adding debugging information such as traces and skeletons to the context of the buggy code.

the following contributions: 1) We introduce a new benchmark for automated debugging, consisting of a collection of 10K Python projects for which we provide passing tests and their corresponding buggy variants.

our model is able to find fixes for a majority of bugs on the QuixBubs benchmark, and on our own benchmark, it is able to find 75% of all bugs in one attempt, and 100% of bugs in two attempts.
we have created a model that is able to fix 68% of bugs in a given repository, with a false positive rate of 5%, and a runtime of one minute.

DeepDebug is a general purpose model that can be used in a variety of debugging scenarios.
we have developed a model that fixes a large number of bugs, with a high success rate and low false positive rate.
DeepDebug can be trained to fix a large number of bugs, and that it can be finetuned to fix a large fraction of bugs that occur in the wild.
The main takeaway from our work is that
transformers can be used to create and repair bugs, but they require a lot of data to work effectively, and they can be further improved by adding debugging information.

a large pretrained transformer model, when finetuned using a small amount of debugging data, can be used to generate a large number of high-quality fixes for bugs that are not easily detected using existing techniques.
transformers are a powerful tool for program repair, and that the use of synthetic data can greatly enhance their performance.
